title: What the tests said, what the phones said and what the company earned
lede: Coca-Cola has never published sales of the 1985 formula as a separate line. What exists is its own research claims, call counts, share figures from trade publications quoted in the press, and the company’s results.

blocks.title: Four figures, four different kinds of source

items.text: **The company’s research**: the margin for the new taste in blind tests of more than 190,000 people, as a spokesman gave it in May 1985.[^4]
**An outside survey**: the share of soft drink buyers who had tasted the new Coke and thought the original was better, per Leo J. Shapiro, a Chicago research firm.[^6]
**The company’s call count**: calls a day to its hotline by June 1985, most of them negative.[^1][^5]
**A later secondary account**: the share at which the new formula settled in its first year.[^16] We could not open a contemporary source for it; treat as unverified.

blocks.title: The drink called “Coke,” from inheritance to nothing
blocks.subtitle: Share of the US soft drink market held by the 1985 formula, in percent. The second point is the share it inherited from the old formula, not one it earned.
blocks.xLabel: Share of US soft drink market (%)

points.title: not on sale
points.text: The formula exists only in tests. Plotted as zero.

points.title: inherits the flagship
points.text: It replaces a drink with 21.7% of the market, per Beverage Digest figures quoted by UPI.[^6]

points.title: the smaller Coke
points.text: With Classic back, it settles at about 3%, by one later account.[^16]

points.title: Coke II
points.text: Sold in a few markets, it “holds onto a 0.1% market share.”[^16]

points.title: withdrawn
points.text: Gone in 2002 or 2004, depending on the source.[^19][^21] Plotted as zero.

blocks.source: UPI, Jul 10, 1985[^6]; Snopes, 1999[^16]. The series mixes a trade figure for the old formula’s share with two figures from a later secondary account, and the end points are plotting conventions. The Coca-Cola Company published no share data for the brand that we found.

blocks.title: Two days of calls about the return equaled 79 ordinary days

left.label: to the hotline in the two days after Coca-Cola Classic was announced[^1]

unit.label: a normal day on the hotline before the change[^1]

blocks.equation: 31,600 ÷ 400 = 79. The match with the 79 days the old formula was gone is a coincidence. Per day: 31,600 ÷ 2 = 15,800, about ten times the 1,500 a day of June 1985.[^1]

blocks.title: The blunder years, on the income statement
blocks.subtitle: The Coca-Cola Company’s net income, in $ millions, as reported by UPI.
blocks.source: 1984: UPI, May 31, 1985 (“a profit of $629 million”).[^4] 1985 and 1986: UPI, Feb 19, 1987.[^11] The 1986 figure includes gains from selling bottling stock and other transactions, which UPI put at 35 cents of the $2.42 a share. These are results for the whole company, including its entertainment business; nothing in them isolates the new formula.

blocks.body: Unknown: sales of the 1985 formula in cases or dollars for any year; what the reformulation, the launch and the reversal cost; and what the 18-month marketing plan was budgeted at. Dyson called it the costliest in the company’s history and gave no number.[^5]
